title: The king who gave himself
hookLine: a boy asks a king for three steps of land, and the king gives his own head; why Kerala welcomes Mahabali home at Onam
carry: bali gave himself: the highest offering
last: PONGAL: THANK THE ONES WHO FEED YOU.

lines: A CIRCLE OF PETALS AT THE DOOR.
BIGGER EVERY MORNING FOR TEN DAYS.
cards: In Kerala, in late summer, on the first morning of Onam, someone gets up early and lays a small circle of flower petals at the front door. Next morning, it grows a ring. And the next.
For ten days it grows, a carpet of flowers called a pookalam, until by the last day it's a bright mandala across the doorstep. A guest is coming. A king, who wants to see that his people are happy.
The same King Bali whose name is in the rakhi prayer.

teach.h: AN ASURA, THE BEST OF KINGS.
teach.b: Mahabali was an asura, from the side usually cast as the gods' rivals. But in Kerala he's remembered as the best king there ever was.
A Malayalam folk song still sung at Onam remembers his reign as a time when all people were equal: no lies, no cheating, no one poor. The gods grew worried about his power.

teach.h: THREE STEPS: EARTH, HEAVEN, HIS HEAD.
teach.b: So Vishnu came to him as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked for just as much land as he could cover in three steps. Bali's own teacher warned him: this boy is Vishnu, don't promise.
Bali, who never refused anyone, said yes anyway. And the boy grew. One step covered the earth.
The second, the heavens. There was nowhere left for the third, so Bali bowed and offered his own head.

The Bhagavata Purana tells it as a story of devotion: Bali is honored, not destroyed, and Vishnu promises to guard his door. Here's the teaching. Bhakti, loving devotion to God, has many forms in the Hindu tradition.
The tradition lists nine, and the last is atma-nivedana, offering yourself. Bali is its classic example. He gave more than land; he gave himself.

Kerala adds one more thing: Bali asked to visit his people once a year, and Onam is that visit. So there's the pookalam, new clothes, and the sadhya, a vegetarian feast on a banana leaf. Keralites of many faiths join in.
And today: Onam asks what you'd hold back from what you love most, and remembers the king who held back nothing.

how: During the ten days of Onam in the Malayalam month of Chingam, many Hindus in Kerala lay a pookalam of flowers at the door that grows each day, wear new clothes, and share the Onam sadhya on banana leaves to welcome King Mahabali, remembered for giving himself to Vishnu as Vamana, on his yearly visit.

games.q: you're King Mahabali. the boy has covered earth and heaven in two steps, and there's nowhere left for the third. you promised. what do you do?
o: offer your own head for the third step.
games.why: he bows and offers his head: atma-nivedana, giving himself. Vishnu honors him, and he asks to visit his people once a year.

practice: Imagine Mahabali is visiting you this year, not to judge, just to see how you are. For each good thing in your life right now, lay one ring of petals at your door, and let the circle grow without rushing it.
Then, if you pray, offer yourself the way Bali did, in your own words: here I am, all of me. If you don't pray, just sit beside the circle like someone waiting for a guest they love.

wordCard.voice: Pongal and Onam. Two harvests: Tamil Nadu's pot boiling over for the sun, and Kerala's flower carpet for a king who comes home once a year.

orig.note: Malayalam: the name of Kerala's harvest festival, in the month of Chingam.

carryVoice: Your line: bali gave himself: the highest offering. And he still comes home. That's day one hundred fifty-four.
